lesson.menu_title: Reading the Room -- Strategic Small Talk and Executive Rapport
lesson.menu_desc: The twelve minutes before the meeting starts, and the mixed conditional -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- Reading the Room
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Denise Gadelha Rocha | Lesson 3 -- Reading the Room

listenings.text: People get one thing wrong about small talk in a second language. They think they have to be charming. Funny, quick, with a good story ready. Nobody expects that. What people actually notice is whether you are interested, and that costs you almost no vocabulary. I have three questions I have used for thirty years. How was the journey. How long are you here for. And the best one: what are you working on at the moment that you actually enjoy? That last one gets you a real answer instead of a job title, and people remember who asked it. One more thing, about silence. When the language is not yours, two seconds of silence feels like twenty. It is not. To everyone else in the room it sounds completely normal. Let it happen. The person who is comfortable with a pause is the one who looks senior.

I run my week in three languages and I still get caught out. If I have spent the whole day in Spanish and then a call starts in English at four in the afternoon, the first ten minutes come out with the wrong shape. The words are English, but the sentences are not. For years I thought that meant I was losing the language. It does not mean that at all. It is simply the price of having three of them. What fixed it was two minutes. Before any call in English, I read something out loud in English, or I listen to two minutes of anything. Two minutes, and the machinery switches over. If I had not built that habit, I would still be spending the first ten minutes of every call apologising and warming up in front of the client, which is the worst possible place to warm up. Now the warming up happens before, on my own, and the client meets the version of me that already works.

extra_audio.text: How was the flight? I did that route in March and the jet lag took me three days. We never catch up properly. Two years of calls and always fifteen minutes. Before the others join, is there anything you want to land today? Let us circle back to that at lunch, when we have proper time.
